Urn A contains 50 red and 50 black balls (known). Urn B contains 100 red and black balls in an unknown ratio. Most people would rather bet on red from Urn A than red from Urn B, AND would also rather bet on black from Urn A than black from Urn B. Is this pair of preferences consistent with holding any single subjective probability for Urn B's colour mix?
choices: Yes — because both bets are safer with a known urn
No — it's inconsistent with any subjective probability; it reflects pure ambiguity aversion instead
No — but only because most urns are red-majority
Yes — Urn B is also exactly 50/50, so the preferences agree

questions.q: In a three-way 'truel,' A never misses, B hits 80% of the time, and C hits 50% of the time. They fire in turn (A, then B, then C, repeating), each shooting at the rival they see as the biggest threat, and A moves first with a free choice: shoot at B, shoot at C, or fire into the air on purpose. Which first move gives A the best chance of survival?
choices: Fire into the air on purpose (deliberately miss)
Shoot at C, the weakest shooter
Shoot at B, the more dangerous shooter
It makes no difference — A's survival odds are the same regardless

questions.q: Bertrand's paradox (the chord version): pick a 'random' chord of a circle and ask for the probability that it's longer than the side of the circle's inscribed equilateral triangle. What's the striking result?
choices: The probability is always exactly 1/2, no matter how the chord is chosen
The probability is always exactly 1/3, no matter how the chord is chosen
There's no single answer — different valid methods of choosing a 'random' chord give different correct probabilities (e.g. 1/3, 1/2, or 1/4)
The question is meaningless, because circles cannot have chords longer than their inscribed triangle's side

questions.q: In Newcomb's paradox, a predictor has already either put $1,000,000 in Box B (if it predicted you'll take only B) or left it empty (if it predicted you'll take both boxes); Box A always visibly holds $1,000. 'Dominance reasoning' says: since the money is already placed, taking both boxes always nets you $1,000 more than taking Box B alone, whatever's inside. 'Expected-utility reasoning', given the predictor's high accuracy, favours taking only Box B. What does this paradox chiefly illustrate?
choices: That two-boxing is objectively the mathematically correct choice in all versions
That one-boxing is objectively the mathematically correct choice in all versions
Two seemingly sound decision-theory principles — dominance and expected-utility maximisation — can recommend opposite choices in the very same problem
That the predictor described in the setup is logically impossible

questions.q: The Doomsday Argument reasons that, treating yourself as a random observer among all humans who will ever be born, the roughly 100 billion humans born so far gives a Bayesian reason to doubt that vastly many more humans (say, another 100 trillion) will ever be born — nudging the expected 'doomsday' earlier. Which principle does this argument rest on?
choices: The law of large numbers applied to historical birth-rate statistics
Confirmed trends in declining global fertility rates
The self-sampling assumption: you should reason as if randomly selected from your reference class of observers
Direct astronomical data on asteroid-impact probabilities

A fair coin lands heads 5 times in a row. A gambler bets on tails, reasoning 'tails is due.' Is this good reasoning?
choices: Yes — after 5 heads in a row, tails becomes statistically more likely
No — the coin has no memory; P(tails) is still 0.5 on the next flip regardless of the streak
Yes, but only because 5 heads in a row is extremely rare
No — the streak actually makes heads more likely to continue

A crime-scene DNA profile matches 1 in 1,000,000 people at random. The suspect's DNA matches. The prosecutor argues this means there is only a 1-in-1,000,000 chance the suspect is innocent. What is wrong with this reasoning?
choices: Nothing is wrong — 1 in 1,000,000 does mean the suspect is almost certainly guilty
It confuses P(match | innocent) with P(innocent | match) — without knowing the size of the potential suspect pool, the match rate alone doesn't give the probability of guilt
The DNA test itself must be flawed if this reasoning seems wrong
The reasoning is wrong only if the suspect has an identical twin
